t: Minimum Degree of a Connected Trio in a Graph - Triangle Enumeration with Degree Arithmetic
o: A connected trio is simply a triangle, and its degree counts the edges leaving it: if the members have degrees d1, d2, d3, the score is d1+d2+d3-6, because each member spends exactly two incident edges on internal connections. Example 1 has the lone triangle {1,2,3} with degrees 3, 3, 3, giving 9-6 = 3. Example 2 shows the minimization nuance: {1,4,3} scores 0 while {2,5,6} and {5,6,7} score 2, so the answer is 0. Constraints are friendly - n <= 400 with up to n*(n-1)/2 (about 80,000) edges - so checking triples against an O(1)-lookup adjacency matrix already fits, and edge-driven enumeration wastes less work on non-edges. Besides the arithmetic, the only trap is returning -1 when no triangle exists.
k: degree(trio) = deg(a) + deg(b) + deg(c) - 6: each triangle edge is counted twice across the three endpoint degrees.
An adjacency matrix makes 'are u and v adjacent?' O(1), so verifying a candidate trio costs three lookups.
Enumerate triangles through edges - intersect the neighborhoods of an edge's endpoints - to skip pairs that were never adjacent.

a.i: Build the matrix, then examine every combination x < y < z. Bail out immediately unless adj[x][y]; otherwise two more lookups decide whether {x,y,z} is a trio and the degree formula scores it in O(1). At n = 400 there are under 1.1*10^7 ordered triples, so the pruned triple loop is comfortably fast despite cubic asymptotics.
s: Build an adjacency matrix and a degree array from the edge list.
Loop x < y < z; skip unless adj[x][y].
If adj[x][z] and adj[y][z], update the answer with deg[x]+deg[y]+deg[z]-6.
Return the answer, or -1 if nothing was ever recorded.
a.t: O(n^3) worst case - every ordered triple tested once with O(1) checks; about 10^7 iterations at n = 400.
a.sp: O(n^2) space for the adjacency matrix.

a.i: Every trio contains three edges, so walking the edge list (u, v) and asking 'which w is adjacent to both endpoints?' finds all triangles while touching only real edges. For each edge we scan the adjacency list of whichever endpoint has smaller degree and confirm membership of w in the other endpoint's neighborhood via the matrix. Trios get discovered several times (once per contained edge), which is harmless when taking a minimum but would matter if counting.
s: Build adjacency lists, the adjacency matrix, and degrees.
For each edge (u, v), set src to the endpoint with the smaller degree list and dst to the other.
For each w in nbr[src], test adj[w][dst] (self-loops are absent, so w = dst fails the test naturally).
Update the best with deg[u]+deg[v]+deg[w]-6 on success; return best or -1.
a.t: O(E * n) hard worst case, typically much less - per edge only the smaller adjacency list is scanned (O(E * sqrt(E))-style bounds apply); fast at the given limits.
a.sp: O(n^2) for the matrix plus O(E) for adjacency lists.

w: Derive the '-6' aloud before coding - fumbling the internal-edge accounting is the classic error. Other pitfalls: answering 0 instead of -1 for triangle-free graphs, and forgetting that duplicate discoveries are fine for minimization but wrong for counting trios (there you would enforce x < y < z or orient edges). Given n <= 400, open with the matrix triple loop and offer edge-centric enumeration as the complexity-aware upgrade. Follow-ups: count all trios, maximize the trio degree, or generalize to listing k-cliques.
